stories.why: Carney wants Canada to rely less on the US because of President Trump’s tariffs, and closer trade with China is a big part of that plan. The deal also shows China building ties with a close US ally just before Trump arrives in Shenzhen.

The deal builds on a trade truce the two leaders agreed in January. Canada says it has restored market access for more than 90% of the trade that had been hit by tariffs.

stories.summary: A very large crowd gathered in Prague on Sunday 15 November to oppose Prime Minister Andrej Babiš’s plan to change how public TV and radio are funded. Media estimates put the crowd at 350,000 to 400,000.
stories.why: Critics fear the plan would make public broadcasters depend on the government and weaken their independence. The rally also turned into a wider protest against the Babiš government.

stories.headline: Five EU countries plan a centre in Rwanda for rejected asylum seekers
stories.summary: Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands announced on Monday 16 November a plan for a joint deportation centre in Rwanda. It would be the first such facility outside the European Union.
stories.why: Migration is one of the biggest political issues in Europe. The plan shows governments moving to tougher rules, while critics say it could weaken protections for vulnerable people.

event.t: The five countries presented the plan in Vienna on Monday 16 November. It would be the first deportation centre of its kind outside the EU.
The centre is meant for people who have no right to stay and cannot be sent back to their own country, for example because that country refuses to take them back.
The scheme is still being negotiated with Rwanda. People sent there could return home, settle in Rwanda or go to another country where they have a right to stay, Rwanda’s government said.
It would start in 2027 as a pilot with about 100 places.
Rights groups condemned the plan, saying it would leave vulnerable people at risk of abuse.

stories.headline: Inflation rises to 4.0% in the euro area and 3.6% in the UK, driven by energy
stories.summary: Eurostat confirmed on Wednesday 18 November that euro area inflation rose to 4.0% in October, up from 3.8% in September. UK inflation rose to 3.6% from 3.5%, the Office for National Statistics said the same day.
stories.why: When prices rise faster, household budgets are squeezed and central banks are less likely to cut interest rates. Energy prices are the main driver in both the euro area and the UK.

event.t: Euro area annual inflation was 4.0% in October, up from 3.8% in September and 2.1% a year earlier, Eurostat said.
In Eurostat’s first estimate, energy prices were 20.8% higher than a year earlier, the biggest driver. Services prices rose 3.3%.

In the UK, consumer prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5%, the Office for National Statistics said. Fuel prices were again a major cause. Core inflation, which leaves out energy and food, was 2.8%.
The European Commission expects euro area inflation to peak above 4% between late 2026 and early 2027 and then ease, it said in its autumn forecast on 17 November.

event.t: On Sunday 15 November, Bahrain said its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian air attacks before they reached their targets. Sirens and explosions were reported across the country.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they attacked a US military base in Bahrain in response to what they called hostile US actions. Iranian state media said six drones were aimed at a US air-defence radar at a helicopter base.

It is the second such claim in three days. On 13 November the Guards said they had hit a US early-warning radar in Bahrain. The US military denied this and said it shot down two drones with no damage.
It is the first time since September that Bahrain’s air defences have had to stop attacks like this.

stories.sh: Nvidia beats forecasts after CEO exit
stories.headline: Nvidia’s sales double and beat forecasts in its first results since its CEO quit
stories.summary: Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the three months to 25 October, up 103% from a year earlier, on Tuesday 17 November. It forecast sales above analysts’ estimates for the next quarter, in its first results since chief executive Jensen Huang resigned.
stories.why: Nvidia makes most of the chips used to build artificial intelligence, so its results show whether the AI boom is still going. They came after a week of turmoil over its leadership and a sharp fall in US tech stocks.

event.t: Revenue was $115.8 billion in the quarter to 25 October, up 103% from a year earlier. Revenue from data centres, mostly AI chips, was $107.6 billion.

Nvidia expects about $130 billion in revenue next quarter, plus or minus 3%. Analysts had expected $125.25 billion on average, Reuters reports, citing LSEG data. The forecast assumes no sales of data-centre chips in China.
Interim chief executive Colette Kress said the company’s “momentum is real”. The Washington Post notes the results did little to answer questions about Nvidia’s future after Huang’s exit.

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday 12 November, the company’s board said. It followed reports of affairs, including one with a woman US intelligence agencies suspect of spying for China.
Chief financial officer Colette Kress is interim chief executive while the company looks for a permanent replacement.
On Monday 16 November the S&P 500 fell 1.9% and the Nasdaq 2.5%. Nvidia shares fell 4.1% to $156.14, their lowest close since July 2025, CNN reports.

stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin are due to hold their first three-way meeting in China on Thursday
stories.summary: The leaders of the US, China and Russia are due to meet together for the first time on Thursday 19 November, in Shenzhen, during the APEC summit. The White House says the main topic is reducing nuclear weapons.
stories.why: The US, Russia and China are the world’s biggest nuclear powers, and their three leaders have never met as a group. What they agree, or fail to agree, could shape arms control for years. The meeting also comes while the wars in Ukraine and Iran are still going on.
stories.simple: The presidents of the United States, China and Russia plan to sit down together on Thursday in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. It would be the first time the three meet as a group. The US says it wants to talk about having fewer nuclear weapons.

event.t: The White House said on Friday 13 November that President Trump will meet China’s leader Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin together. It would be the first three-way meeting of the countries’ leaders.
The Kremlin said the meeting will be held on 19 November in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC summit. China’s foreign ministry confirmed the place and the day on Monday 16 November.
The White House says Trump wants to discuss reducing the number of nuclear weapons in the world.
US officials told ABC News that Trump expects to discuss Iran with Xi and Putin, but does not plan to discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine at the three-way meeting.

effects.t: A joint commitment on nuclear weapons by the three powers would be new. No three-way agreement of this kind exists today.

stories.summary: Britain imposed sanctions on Tuesday 17 November on eight Israeli construction and property companies that build settlements in the occupied West Bank. It also targeted Tzav 9, a group it accuses of blocking aid trucks to Gaza.
stories.why: It is Britain’s first concrete step since it said in September it would respond to faster settlement growth. The UK says it wants to keep a future Palestinian state possible. Relations between the UK and Israel have grown tense over the war in Gaza and settlement building.

stories.headline: US moves to stop Chinese firms from using American AI chips through data centres abroad
stories.summary: The US Commerce Department issued a rule on Monday 16 November that requires licences for advanced AI chips sent to data centres in five countries. The aim is to stop Chinese companies from using American chips remotely.
stories.why: Advanced chips are the key resource for building AI. The US wants to keep the most powerful ones away from China, and data centres in other countries had become a way around the existing rules. The new rule affects chip makers, cloud companies and several Asian economies.

event.t: The interim rule requires data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil to get a US licence before receiving advanced AI chips from Nvidia and other US makers.
Companies will also need a licence to send AI chips to data centres anywhere in the world if they may provide computing power to companies in China or other restricted countries.
The rule follows closer scrutiny of US chip export policy after an alleged spying scandal involving Nvidia, Bloomberg reports.
